title: Signature Capability Card
body:
The Signature Capability Card is Manon's original design for a one-card summary of what an AI tool at work can and cannot do. Each card carries four lines in plain words: what the tool is good at, what it is poor at, what must always be checked, and who owns the final result. The card travels with the tool: it is shown before first use, pinned where the tool is opened, and updated whenever the tool changes. Its purpose is to replace vague impressions, such as the tool is smart or the tool is risky, with a short, shared, checkable statement that every worker on a team can read in under a minute and act on the same way.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-line card design. First, the good-at line names two or three task types the tool handles well, in the team's own words, such as drafting and summarizing. Second, the poor-at line names the failure territory, such as facts, dates, and judgments about people. Third, the must-check line names what is always checked before use, without duplicating the companion checking method, which the card points to rather than repeats. Fourth, the owner line names the human role that owns the final result, never the tool itself. The demo below assembles a small card from its four lines and counts them, which is the completeness check a team runs before issuing a card.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature capability card. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: good at: drafting, summarizing; poor at: facts, judgments; must check: names, numbers, dates; owner: named human; card lines: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team adopting an AI tool, as the first page of team guidance for that tool. Do not use it as a safety claim about a real public product, because the card is a Signature design, not a certification of any tool. Do not use it as a substitute for reading the employer's actual policy, because the card summarizes team practice and the policy remains the governing document. title: Signature Failure Atlas
body:
The Signature Failure Atlas is Manon's original design for a team's shared map of how AI tools fail at work. The atlas is a simple wall chart or page with one row per failure mode: the mode's name in plain words, a real example from the team's own work with names removed, the tell-tale sign that gives it away, and the response, which is always to pause and check through the companion method. Teams add a row each time a new failure appears, so the atlas grows from experience rather than from theory, and new joiners learn from the team's actual mistakes instead of repeating them. The atlas is deliberately public inside the team: hidden failures repeat, while mapped failures get caught.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-column atlas design. First, the name column uses plain words, such as invented reference or stale rule, so anyone can use it. Second, the example column carries one anonymized real case, because an abstract warning is forgettable and a real case is not. Third, the sign column names what to look for, such as a reference nobody can open or a rule that contradicts a current document. Fourth, the response column always points the same way: pause, do not forward, and check through the companion verifying method. The demo below lists a small atlas and counts its rows, which is the growth check a team runs each month.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature failure atlas. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: invented reference -> sign: reference nobody can open; false confidence -> sign: certain tone, no source; stale rule -> sign: contradicts current document; atlas rows: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for teams that already use AI tools and want to learn from errors systematically. Do not use it as a record of blame, because rows must never name the worker who made the error, only the failure and its sign. Do not use it as a complete catalog of all possible failures, because new tools bring new modes, and the atlas is a living map, not a finished one. title: Signature Human Check Gate
body:
The Signature Human Check Gate is Manon's original design for a workflow rule that no AI output passes into use until a named human opens the gate. The gate is not a checking method: it is the checkpoint itself, a visible step in the workflow where output waits, the checker is named, and the gate opens only when the checker stamps it. The design's insight is that checking fails most often not because workers do not know how to check, but because no step in the workflow ever asks them to, so output flows straight from tool to customer or record. The gate inserts that missing step, makes it visible, and makes skipping it an exception that must be explained rather than the default.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part gate design. First, the gate sits between generation and use in every AI-assisted workflow, with no path around it. Second, the gate names its checker, who is a person with the time and standing to do the check, not a role nobody holds. Third, the gate records its stamp: who checked, when, and through which checking method, pointing to the companion verifying-ai-outputs pair for the method itself. Fourth, the gate has a hold rule: anything the checker is unsure about stays held and is escalated, never released on the assumption that it is probably fine. The demo below shows a small batch waiting at a gate and counts how many are still held, which is the number a manager watches.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature human check gate. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: memo draft - stamped; client reply - held; report table - held; held at gate: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any AI-assisted workflow where output leaves the team or enters a record. Do not use it as a checking method, because the method lives in the companion pair and the gate deliberately points to it rather than duplicating it. Do not use it as a claim that gated output is correct, because a gate proves a check happened, not that the check caught everything. title: Signature Role Map
body:
The Signature Role Map is Manon's original design for a worker's personal map of how automation touches their own role. The map is a single page divided into three columns: tasks the tool already does, tasks that are changing because of the tool, and tasks that are new, such as checking, handling exceptions, and improving the process. The worker fills it in from their own week, not from a generic job description, and updates it whenever a tool changes. Its value is that it turns a vague feeling about automation into a visible picture, and a visible picture into a plan: the changing and new columns are where the worker's next skills live, and the map shows which one to learn first.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-column map design. First, the worker lists their real weekly tasks, as many as fit on one page, from memory and from their calendar. Second, each task is placed in one column: done by the tool, changing because of the tool, or new because of the tool. Third, the worker marks the column that holds the most judgment, conversation, and exception handling, because that column is the durable part of the role. Fourth, the worker picks one skill from the changing or new column, names a small real task to practice it on, and dates the practice. The demo below sorts a small week into the three columns and counts each, which is the map in miniature.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature role map. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: tool does: 2; changing: 1; new: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design in personal planning, in manager-worker conversations, and in team automation discussions. Do not use it as a prediction about any particular job, because maps describe one worker's week and cannot promise an outcome. Do not use it to rank workers against each other, because its purpose is personal planning, not comparison. title: Signature Privacy Dial for Work
body:
The Signature Privacy Dial for Work is Manon's original design for a simple control that shows, at a glance, how much protection a piece of work material needs before it goes into an AI tool. The dial has three positions: green for public material that may be entered freely, amber for internal material that may be entered only in an approved tool, and red for sensitive material that must never be entered into an outside tool. The worker sets the dial by asking one question about the material: what happens if it leaves the organization? If the answer is nothing, the dial is green; if it is embarrassment or commercial harm, amber; if it is harm to a person, a breach of trust, or a broken agreement, red. The dial is deliberately physical in its metaphor, so the decision is felt as a setting, not lost in fine print.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-position dial design. First, the material is sorted by the harm question, not by its format, because a short note can be red and a long document green. Second, the dial position decides the tool: green uses any tool, amber uses only an approved tool, red uses no outside tool at all. Third, amber and red material is redacted before any use, with placeholders replacing names, numbers, and case details. Fourth, the dial is rechecked whenever material is combined, because two green pieces can combine into an amber or red picture. The demo below sorts a small set of items onto the dial and counts the red ones, which are the items that must never be pasted.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature privacy dial for work. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: public brochure -> green; team rota -> amber; customer record -> red; salary note -> red; red items (never paste): 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a training aid and a desk reminder for workers who use AI tools. Do not use it as legal advice about privacy or confidentiality, because the dial is a habit aid and the governing rules are the employer's policy and the applicable law. Do not use it to claim redacted material is always safe, because combinations can still identify people or cases. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Signature Oversight Chair
body:
The Signature Oversight Chair is Manon's original design for the idea that every AI-assisted workflow has one named human sitting in the chair of responsibility, and the chair is never empty while the workflow runs. The chair is a role, not a person: it is filled by whoever is on duty for that workflow, it is handed over explicitly with a note of what is in flight, and it is visible to the whole team, so anyone can see who is in charge of a given output at a given moment. The design answers the most common oversight failure, which is not malice but diffusion: five people each assumed someone else was checking, so nobody was. With the chair, there is always one name, and the name is always findable.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part chair design. First, every AI-assisted workflow names its chair before it starts, and the chair's name is written where the work is tracked. Second, the chair holds three duties: deciding what the tool is asked, ensuring the output is checked through the companion method, and being able to stop the workflow. Third, the chair is handed over in writing, with open items listed, so a change of shift never leaves the chair empty. Fourth, the chair's decisions are logged in one line each, so responsibility is traceable later without a hunt through messages. The demo below shows a small duty roster and flags the workflow with no chair, which is the gap to fix first.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature oversight chair. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: client replies -> chair: Ana; report summaries -> chair: EMPTY - assign before running; internal drafts -> chair: Ben; empty chairs: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team running AI-assisted workflows, and in training on accountability. Do not use it as a way to blame the chair for every error, because the chair owns the checking process, while the team still owns its own work, and blame would stop people volunteering for the chair. Do not use it as a substitute for the checking method, which lives in the companion pair. title: Signature Policy Page
body:
The Signature Policy Page is Manon's original design for a one-page version of a workplace AI policy that workers can actually use at the moment of use. A full policy is long and legal, which means it is read once and never consulted again; the Policy Page distills it into five lines the worker needs: approved tools, never-enter data, disclosure duty, checking duty, and escalation route. The page is produced by the team from the real policy, checked against it, and kept where the work happens, such as pinned beside the tool or printed at the desk. When the policy changes, the page changes the same day, and the old page is removed, so there is never a choice between two versions.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-line distillation design. First, the team reads the real policy together and extracts one line per question, in the team's own words. Second, each line is checked back against the policy by a second reader, so the distillation cannot drift into invention. Third, the page is placed where the tool is opened, not filed in a folder, because a page consulted at the moment of use is the only kind that changes behavior. Fourth, the page carries its date and the policy version it distills, so staleness is visible. Fifth, the page is reviewed whenever the policy changes or a new tool is approved. The demo below checks a small page for its five lines and names the missing one.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature policy page. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: page lines present: 4 of 5; missing line: ['checking duty'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team governed by an AI policy, as a companion to the policy rather than a replacement for it. Do not use it as legal advice or as a substitute for reading the full policy when a serious question arises, because the page is a summary and the policy governs. Do not use it to invent rules the policy does not contain, because a page that adds rules will be distrusted and then ignored. title: Signature Fairness Lens
body:
The Signature Fairness Lens is Manon's original design for a simple check workers apply when an AI tool helps judge people at work. The lens has three panes, and a recommendation about a person must pass all three before a human acts on it. The first pane asks whether outcomes differ systematically across groups, not just in single cases. The second pane asks whether the recommendation can be explained in plain language, without hiding behind the tool. The third pane asks whether the input data itself might be skewed, for example reflecting who received the good assignments rather than who did good work. A recommendation that fails any pane goes to human review, and the human decision is recorded separately from the tool's suggestion, so the tool never becomes the decision-maker by default.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-pane lens design. First, the worker gathers the outcomes the tool produced, grouped in whatever way the team is permitted to examine, and looks for systematic gaps. Second, the worker writes the tool's reasons in their own words, and if they cannot, the recommendation is flagged for review. Third, the worker asks what history the tool learned from and whether that history could carry an old unfairness forward. Fourth, the human decision is written down with its own reasons, so the record shows a human decided, not a tool. The demo below shows a small set of group scores and flags the gap that needs investigation before any action.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature fairness lens. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: group A 80; group B 79; group C 52; gap to investigate: 28 points Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design in training for hiring, management, and customer-facing roles, and whenever AI assists a judgment about a person. Do not use it as legal advice about discrimination law, because the lens is a habit aid and the law turns on specific facts and jurisdictions. Do not use it to declare a tool fair on the strength of one pane passing, because all three panes must pass together. title: Signature Never-Enter List
body:
The Signature Never-Enter List is Manon's original design for a short, memorable, team-owned list of material that never goes into an outside AI tool. The list has five entries, each in plain words: credentials and keys, other people's personal data, unreleased commercial material, material under a confidentiality promise, and anything whose disclosure would break trust. The list is posted where AI tools are used, rehearsed in onboarding with examples, and tested in practice: new joiners are shown sample prompts and asked which entries each prompt would break. The design's strength is brevity: a list of five can be remembered under deadline pressure, while a policy of fifty cannot, and remembered rules are the ones that get followed.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-entry list design. First, the team writes its list from its real risks, starting from the five entries above and adjusting only with care. Second, the list is posted where tools are opened and printed for desks where that helps. Third, onboarding rehearses it with sample prompts, including tricky ones where a prompt seems harmless but contains a name or a case detail that identifies someone. Fourth, the list is reviewed when a new tool is approved or a new kind of material arrives, so it never goes stale. Fifth, a breach of the list is reported through the employer's incident route at once, because early reporting limits harm and the list's purpose is prevention, not punishment. The demo below screens a small prompt and counts its violations.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature never-enter list. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: customer name -> on list; public description -> not on list; access key -> on list; violations: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a desk aid and onboarding rehearsal for any team using AI tools. Do not use it as a guarantee that everything not on the list is safe, because combinations of allowed details can still identify a person or a case. Do not use it to handle a breach quietly, because quiet handling leaves the disclosure uncontained. title: Signature Skill Ladder
body:
The Signature Skill Ladder is Manon's original design for a reskilling path drawn as a ladder with visible rungs, so a worker can see where they stand and what the next step is. The bottom rung is the worker's current strength, the middle rungs are the supervising and exception-handling skills the automated process actually needs, and the top rung is the ability to improve the process itself. Each rung names one skill, one real task to practice it on, and one piece of evidence that it worked, such as a checked batch, a resolved exception, or a process fix adopted by the team. The ladder is personal: it is built from the worker's own role map, reviewed with their manager, and climbed one rung at a time, so progress is visible and the next step is never a mystery.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-rung ladder design. First, the worker and manager agree the starting rung from current strengths. Second, they pick the next rung as the skill the team needs most that the worker can build on fastest. Third, the worker practices it on a small supervised real task, not a generic exercise. Fourth, the evidence is recorded on the ladder itself, so the ladder becomes a portfolio. Fifth, the ladder is reviewed at a fixed rhythm, such as every six weeks, and the next rung is chosen from what the review shows. title: Signature Concern Letter
body:
The Signature Concern Letter is Manon's original design for a short, structured way for a worker to raise an AI concern in writing. The letter has four paragraphs: the specific case, with date, tool, and output; the effect on the work; the risk if it continues; and one proposed fix within the manager's power. Its structure matters because managers act faster on one clear case with one fix than on a general worry, and because a written letter creates a dated record of what was raised, which protects both the worker and the manager if the issue later matters. The letter is deliberately calm in tone: it describes work and risk, not motives, and it invites a fix rather than demanding a verdict on AI in general.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-paragraph letter design. First, the case paragraph names the date, the tool, the output, and what went wrong, in facts rather than adjectives. Second, the effect paragraph states what the case cost: delayed work, a customer impact, a risk to a record, or rework time. Third, the risk paragraph states what happens if the pattern continues, in the same concrete terms. Fourth, the fix paragraph proposes one change, such as a checking step, a pause for one task type, or a policy clarification, and asks for a review date. The letter is sent, kept by the worker with its date, and followed up if no reply arrives by the review date. The demo below assembles a small letter outline and counts its paragraphs, which is the completeness check before sending.

Use and limits. Use this design before raising an AI concern at work, and in training on raising concerns well. Do not use it as legal advice about employment rights or formal reporting, which differ by jurisdiction; this record is educational reference only. Do not use it to avoid the formal reporting route where safety, privacy, or fair treatment is at stake, because the letter complements that route and does not replace it. title: Signature Oversight Rhythm
body:
The Signature Oversight Rhythm is Manon's original design for a small, regular team review that keeps AI-assisted work checked and improving. The rhythm has four beats, repeated weekly or per project: what AI-assisted work is in flight and who chairs each piece, what errors or near-misses were found since last time, what tool or policy change is needed, and what the team learned, written in one paragraph where new joiners can read it. The rhythm is deliberately short, fifteen minutes for a busy team, because a short review that happens beats a long governance meeting that is postponed. Its product is not a document but a habit: a team that reviews its own AI work regularly catches its errors earlier each month, and its learning note becomes the team's memory.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part rhythm design. First, the rhythm is fixed: weekly for busy teams, per-project for slower ones, never longer than a month apart. Second, the attendees are the people who actually check AI work, not only managers. Third, the inputs are fixed: the list of AI-assisted outputs, the errors found, and the policy or tool questions raised. Fourth, the outputs are fixed: named fixes with owners and dates, plus one learning paragraph. Fifth, the escalation is fixed: which findings go to management, to the policy owner, or to the formal route, and by when. The demo below shows a small rhythm agenda and flags the item without an owner, which is the rhythm's first fix.

Do not use it as a replacement for the checking method in the companion verifying-ai-outputs pair, which supplies the steps used inside the rhythm's checks. title: Signature Risk Board
body:
The Signature Risk Board is Manon's original design for a visible board where a team tracks the risks of automating a work process. The board has five rows, one per risk: wrong outputs reaching customers or records, sensitive data leaking through the tool, workers losing the skill to do the task by hand, unfair treatment by the automated step, and loss of accountability when nobody can explain a decision. Each row carries a likelihood, a seriousness, a countermeasure, and an owner, and rows are reviewed whenever the tool, the data, or the team changes. The board's rule is plain: a serious risk without a countermeasure means the process is not ready to automate, whatever its promised savings, and the board stays visible until that row is fixed.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-row board design. First, the people who actually do the work list the process steps the automation would touch. Second, for each touched step, the team names the worst plausible failure and who it would affect. Third, likelihood and seriousness are rated in simple terms: low, medium, or high. Fourth, each medium or high risk gets a countermeasure and an owner, chosen from checking, limiting, falling back to manual work, or excluding the step from automation. Fifth, the board is reviewed at a fixed date, because risks change as tools and teams change. The demo below scores three risks and flags the one that is both likely and serious, which is the board's first fix.

The output reads: wrong output - high / high -> FIX FIRST; data leak - low / high -> monitor; skill loss - medium / medium -> monitor Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design before automating a process, when an automated process starts erring, and in team discussions about new tools. Do not use it as a formal compliance assessment, because regulated sectors have their own duties, and this record is educational reference only. Do not use it to approve automation on a low average risk, because one high-seriousness risk without a countermeasure outweighs several low ones. title: Signature Worker File
body:
The Signature Worker File is Manon's original design for a personal file a worker keeps about how AI touches their own work. The file has four sections: a tool note naming the AI tools that touch the worker's work and the policy rules for each, a decision note for any AI-assisted decision about the worker, a concern note for any worry raised, to whom, on what date, and with what response, and a recourse note naming the internal route, the worker representative, and the external route that applies, written down before they are needed. The file is kept outside any system the employer alone controls, in a form the worker can still reach after changing roles, and it is kept factual: dates, quotes, and documents, not characterizations of people's motives. A worker with such a file is never reconstructing history from memory during a dispute.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-section file design. First, the tool note is written when a tool is first used and updated when policy changes. Second, the decision note is written whenever an AI-assisted decision about the worker occurs, with the explanation given. Third, the concern note is written the day a concern is raised, with the response when it arrives. Fourth, the recourse note is written in calm time, not during a dispute, so the routes are known before they are needed. The file is reviewed by the worker alone, and it contains only material about the worker's own work, never other people's private data. The demo below checks a small file for its four sections and names the missing one.

Use and limits. Use this design in worker training, representative briefings, and personal planning. Do not use it as legal advice, because employment and data rights differ by jurisdiction and contract, and anyone facing a real dispute should seek qualified advice promptly. Do not use it to collect other people's private data, because a personal file about one's own work is legitimate record-keeping, while gathering colleagues' data is not. title: Signature Circle Keeper
body:
The Signature Circle Keeper is Manon's original design for a role that guards the circle of confidentiality around restricted material when AI tools are in use. The Keeper is a named person or a small team function that answers one question for colleagues: may this material leave the circle, and through which tool? The Keeper holds the list of agreements, the employer's policy, and the approved-tool list, and gives answers in writing, so workers do not have to interpret confidentiality duties alone under deadline pressure. The Keeper does not slow work down in practice, because most questions have quick answers, and the slow cases are exactly the ones where a pause is worth more than speed. The design's promise is that no worker has to guess about confidentiality alone.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-question keeper design. First, what agreement or duty covers this material, and who is inside its circle? Second, does the employer's policy name the proposed tool as approved for this class of material, in writing? Third, does the tool's data handling keep the material inside the circle, or retain, reuse, or route it elsewhere? Fourth, if any answer is unclear, what approved alternative exists, such as an internal tool, a redacted version, or manual work, and who can give the permission needed? A question the Keeper cannot answer is itself an answer: the material stays inside until it can be answered, and the question and its answer are recorded for the next worker. The demo below runs three checks and gives the verdict they imply.

Use and limits. Use this design for teams handling client, patient, legal, or commercially sensitive material, and in onboarding for such roles. Do not use it as legal advice about any specific agreement, which must be read in full and, where stakes are high, reviewed by a qualified adviser. Do not use it to argue that a popular tool is safe, because popularity says nothing about where entered material goes. title: Signature Literacy Page
body:
The Signature Literacy Page is Manon's original design for a worker's personal one-page AI literacy plan. The page has five lines: the tools the worker actually uses and the policy rule for each, the failure modes to watch for in their tasks, the privacy screen run before prompting, the checking route used through the companion verifying-ai-outputs pair, and the next skill to build as automation changes their role. The page is written in one sitting, kept where the worker works, and reviewed monthly with their manager: which lines held, which failed, and what to change. A page built this way is personal in the useful sense: it names real tools, real tasks, and a real next skill, rather than repeating generic guidance, and its monthly review is how literacy becomes a habit instead of a course attended once.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-line page design. First, list tools and policy rules, one line per tool. Second, write a personal failure watchlist of the two failure modes most likely in the worker's tasks. Third, write the privacy screen as three reminders actually run before prompting. Fourth, name the checking route: the companion method plus the person who checks consequential work alongside the worker. Fifth, name one next skill tied to automation in the role, with a start date and a small real task to prove it. The page is reviewed monthly, and lines that repeatedly fail are redesigned rather than repeated. The demo below tracks a small page by line status, which is the monthly review in miniature.

Do not use it as a certificate or a claim of competence, because literacy is shown by checked work over time, not by a completed page. Do not use it to replace team oversight, because a personal page supports the team's routine and does not substitute for it.
